A new study from the NAB FASTROAD (Flexible Advanced Services for Television & Radio on All Devices) technology advocacy program found that the adoption of an industry standard for delivering content to mobile devices could lead to $2 billion in revenue for the broadcast television industry by 2012, TVnewsday reports.
According to NAB’s “Study of the Impact of Multiple Systems for Mobile/Handheld Digital Television,” the success of mobile TV services can reach its full potential if a mobile/handheld digital TV standard from the Advanced Television Standards Committee is released – and universally adopted – by early next year.
If such a standard is adopted quickly and results in the forecast $2 billion, local stations, TV networks and syndicators would share in the revenue, the report says. This potential revenue will come from new forms of advertising, over-the-air programs offered for a fee on mobile devices and partnerships with mobile service operators.
More details, including the complete report, can be found here
explanation:
Blog/news post summarizing an industry report, following a structured format of report details, scope, and projections for broadband in financial services.

The article has referenced the NATA report findings and a summary form, meaning the sentence ending with "More details... can be found here" strongly implies an inline hyperlink or URL accompanies it.

Final token "here" is part of "Additional information about the study, including the actual report, can be found here" — a classic hyperlink anchor phrase in news/blog writing, expecting either a period, punctuation, or a linked URL/marker immediately after.
"The Wireless Applications Committee of the National Association of Broadcasters recently issued an eight-page report..." and supporting study details build toward this closing sentence. "More details on the report and a certain partnership proposal can be found here" concludes.

source_text: Some individuals may not be familiar with the term “closed-head injuries,” and accordingly, they might not be aware of its meaning. Closed-head injuries are a kind of traumatic brain injury (TBI) that doesn’t involve any object penetration into the skull and brain. Instead, it could be a physical blow to the head, or even a blow to the body, that could make the head move quickly back and forth such that it could bounce the brain around on the inside of the skull
explanation:
Medical/health informational content establishing educational tone, defining TBI for a general public audience.
